name: TAMERA OBIAGERI OKAFOR
missingPieces: D2 SQL injection CVSS uses A:H giving 9.8; the auth bypass does not affect availability so the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. D3 per-finding CVSS lines in the F1-F7 body are left as the empty template CVSS:3.1/AV/AC/PR/UI/S/C/I/A, though the full vectors are supplied in the later table.
feedback: D1 is a near-complete catalogue and the strongest part of this submission. You found all ten canonical vulnerabilities, each with a quoted source line or capture line and a correct or defensible OWASP plus CWE pairing: the SQL injection at lines 65 to 66 with the concatenated WHERE clause, the alg:none acceptance with Token 2, the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 at line 30, the missing exp claim on Tokens 1 and 3, unsalted MD5, the XXE SYSTEM file read, path traversal at 02:24:02 returning root:x:0:0, the stored XSS cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9 at 02:18:47, the open redirect at 02:21:13, and the cookie missing Secure and SameSite. One small label slip: you tagged path traversal as A02 Broken Access Control when Broken Access Control is A01, but the CWE-22 and the evidence line are right so it keeps credit. You also nailed the decoy by naming hash_equals at line 53, ruling it not exploitable, and proving it at the mechanism level as constant-time comparison while correctly pointing to alg:none as the real bug. D2 is strong. The chain runs in order with each hop reconciled to a timestamp, the PoC payloads are verbatim, and the scope-change insight is captured in the paragraph about JWT forgery reaching dependent services that trust the token. The one real error is the SQL injection CVSS: you used A:H to reach 9.8, but the authentication bypass does not impair availability, so the vector should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N for about 9.1. Your impact work is exactly what was wanted, with the 20-row sample averaged to about 202,011.60 naira, extrapolated to 312 customers for 63,027,619 naira, the assumption stated plainly, and the BoltCash launch tied in. D3 is polished: the executive summary is jargon-free and ends on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model names the external attacker and the shared JWT trust, the decoy is restated correctly, the chain ends on the earliest-break SQLi fix, the remediation table is genuinely ordered by risk reduction per hour with effort estimates rather than raw severity, and both detection stopgaps give a concrete field and a false-positive rate. The only blemish is that the CVSS lines inside the F1 to F7 bodies are left as the empty template string, though you do supply the full vectors in the table that follows. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 canon I by number as load-bearing, names NDPA section 40 tied to the breached customers, and anchors to your own findings; watch the slip where you wrote 313 customers instead of 312. Nothing here is fabricated; every figure and line traces to the evidence pack. This is excellent, near-complete work. The single most important fix is to correct the SQL injection availability metric to A:N so the vector and the score reflect that an auth bypass does not take the service down.
